result.markdown: --- title: "[ConvexPSpline]{.doc-object-name .doc-class .doc-label .doc-label-class}" body-classes: doc-api-page page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Shape-constrained P-spline: convex or concave. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/main/whittaker/smooths/monotone.py#L100-L177){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.CLASS} ```python ConvexPSpline(k=20, degree=3, m=2, concave=False) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Uses the same B-spline basis and difference penalty as `~whittaker.smooths.pspline.PSpline`, but additionally requires the fitted curve `f(x) = \sum_j \beta_j B_j(x)` to be convex (or, with `concave=True`, concave) over the whole domain. As with `MonotonePSpline`, this is enforced as a linear inequality on the coefficients: for an equally-spaced B-spline basis, the curve is convex whenever the second differences of the coefficients, `\Delta^2 \beta_j = \beta_j - 2\beta_{j-1} + \beta_{j-2}`, are all non-negative. Use `ConvexPSpline` (via `s(x, bs="cx")` for convex or `s(x, bs="cv")` for concave in a formula) when the relationship is known to have a single bend of consistent curvature — e.g. a cost curve, a learning curve, or a concave production function — and an unconstrained smooth would otherwise produce spurious inflection points from noise. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[20]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of B-spline basis functions. The default is `20`. [degree]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[3]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : B-spline polynomial degree. The default is `3` (cubic). [m]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[2]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Difference penalty order. The default is `2`. [concave]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, enforce concavity. The default is `False` (convex). ::: ## Notes {.doc-notes} As with `MonotonePSpline`, the constraint is enforced during P-IRLS fitting by projecting the ordinary coefficient update onto the convex (or concave) cone after each iteration: smooth terms whose basis is a `ConvexPSpline` have their coefficient block passed through `project_convex` before the next iteration's linear predictor is formed (see `whittaker.fitting.pirls`). The projection extends the monotone PAVA projection by one order of differencing: convexity requires the *first* differences of the coefficients, `d_j = \beta_j - \beta_{j-1}`, to form a non-decreasing sequence (equivalently, that the second differences of `\beta` are non-negative), so `project_convex` computes the first differences, projects *them* onto the monotone cone with PAVA (see the `Notes` on `MonotonePSpline` for the algorithm), and then reconstructs `\beta` by cumulatively summing the projected differences back up from `\beta_0`. Concavity is handled by negating the differences before and after the PAVA projection, mirroring `decreasing=True` for `MonotonePSpline`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#caf1b661 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import whittaker as wt rng = np.random.default_rng(0) x = np.sort(rng.uniform(-1, 1, 200)) y = x**2 + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=200) model = wt.GAM("y ~ s(x, bs='cx')").fit({"x": x, "y": y}) new_x = np.linspace(-1, 1, 50) fitted = model.predict({"x": new_x}).values second_diff = np.diff(fitted, n=2) # Second differences are non-negative up to fitting/projection tolerance. np.all(second_diff >= -1e-2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` np.True_ ``` ::: :::
